newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president seen blundering towards election.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president seen blundering towards election.

text.p: President Kim Young-sam made a major gaffe by ramming a controversial labour law through South Korea's parliament, and Tuesday's climbdown could erode his authority in his last year in office, analysts said.

They said Kim's concession to reopen parliamentary debate over the law would weaken confidence in the economy, dealing a blow to the ruling New Korea Party in the run-up to presidential elections in December.
"This probably is the biggest blunder of Kim's presidency," said Shin Jung-hyun, a political science professor at Kyunghee University.
"The blunder will increase pressure to turn him into a lame duck and make it difficult for him to maintain full control over setting the political agenda for the rest of his tenure," he said.
Kim's single term expires after the election, but he is expected to try to install a protege in office.
"The law was a gamble aimed at securing the upper hand in the election. This failed and the ruling camp will now be busy controlling the damage," said political commentator Ra Jong-il.
Ra said that by trying to crush worker militancy and help companies regain competitiveness by cutting wage costs, Kim wanted to win support from the middle class and conservatives.
"It is too early to predict an election outcome but the failure in the strategy will undermine Kim's influence," he told Reuters.
In a meeting with opposition leaders to defuse an industrial crisis, Kim admitted the legislation shoved through parliament on December 26 caused public anxiety and hampered the economy.
Forced passage of the bill in a dawn session with no opposition deputies present sparked more than three weeks of wildcat strikes that cost the country more than $3 billion in lost production.
Kim also said he would instruct officials to suspend arrest warrants served on strike leaders, seven of whom are sheltering in Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral.
Kim has previously ruled out any compromise over the law and vowed to enforce the law over wildcat strikes.
The labour law was designed to free up the labour market and thus cut corporate costs and boost competitiveness, but Kim acknowledged that it failed to serve its purpose by triggering strikes.
Lee Hahn-koo, head of the Daewoo Reserach Institute under the giant business conglomerate Daewoo Group, said sending the labour law back to parliament would inject uncertainty into the economy.

"The biggest winner in the whole saga is the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions. With its power boosted unionists are likely to take a hardline stand when they start negotiating for wages and working conditions from spring," Lee said.
"This will make business more difficult, thus further slowing the economy," he added.
Analysts said protracted wrangling over the labour law would haunt the president during election jockeying. Passage of the bill had hurt potential presidential candidates in the ruling party.

"The image of ruling party chairman Lee Hong-koo, for example, was seriously tarnished along with that of President Kim," said Ra. "Former supreme court justice Lee Hoi-chang's image as an uncompromising righteous man has also been marred as he took part in the railroading of the law."
The two Lees have widely been tipped as candidates to be hand-picked by the president.
Kim, the first South Korean president without any military background in decades, built his fame as a reformer but he has come under strong attack for his perceived high-handed authoritarian style.
